c.tagline: Ancient walled city rising again after years of war.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used in practice; agree on the fare with the driver before departing, or have your hotel arrange the ride.

emergency.note: Dispatchers may not speak English; ask hotel staff to help contact emergency services.

avoid.reason: Avoid former front-line suburbs such as Jobar, Yarmouk and parts of Eastern Ghouta, where war damage, unexploded ordnance and checkpoints remain.
Never photograph checkpoints, soldiers or government buildings, carry ID at all times, and expect frequent security checks moving around the city.

hood_desc: UNESCO-listed walled Old City with Roman-era gates, the Umayyad Mosque and winding stone lanes lined with courtyard houses turned boutique hotels, cafes and bars; best for culture-focused travelers who want to be inside the historic core, though rooms are small and utilities can be inconsistent.

Leafy, upscale diplomatic quarter with embassies, UN offices and international restaurants just west of the Old City; the most reliable power, water and security in the city, favored by business travelers, NGO staff and anyone wanting international-standard comfort.

The bustling commercial heart between the Old City and Umayyad Square, packed with shops, street food stalls and the famed covered Hamidiyeh Souq; convenient and walkable but noisier, suited to budget-to-midrange travelers who want to be in the thick of city life.

A quieter Ottoman-era quarter just outside the old walls near the Bahsa transport hub, known for cheap guesthouses and an unpolished, local feel; popular with backpackers and long-stay budget travelers.

Modern, quiet residential district southwest of downtown housing embassies, NGOs and newer hotels with dependable infrastructure; best for travelers who prioritize calm and reliability over proximity to the sights.

water.note: Avoid tap water given damaged infrastructure; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Syrian pounds) directly to the driver or a conductor; there is no citywide smart card or app-based payment system. Fares are very low, typically well under a dollar.
transit.hours: Roughly 6:00-22:00 for most bus and microbus routes; taxis fill in for night travel.
transit.note: No metro or tram; the city relies on buses and shared microbuses, supplemented heavily by taxis.

train: Chemins de Fer Syriens (CFS) domestic rail - service limited/suspended on many lines due to war damage

airport.name: Damascus International Airport (DAM)
airport.drive: 30-45 min (25 km southeast of city center; longer at checkpoints)
rentals: Local agencies at arrivals hall (no major international chains currently operating due to sanctions)

transit.m: Public bus/microbus to Baramkeh station (~45-60 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or about 10% in restaurants and hotels is appreciated, and small tips for porters and drivers are customary.

food.name: Fatteh
food.desc: Toasted flatbread layered with chickpeas, warm garlicky yoghurt, olive oil and pine nuts; the Damascene breakfast, eaten hot from the pan.

places.name: Abu Abdo
places.note: Long-standing fatteh specialist locals name first; go early before the trays run out.

places.name: Beit Jabri
places.note: Historic courtyard house serving classic Damascene breakfasts under the citrus trees.

places.name: Al Khawali
places.note: Grand old-house restaurant with a full traditional mezze and breakfast repertoire.

food.name: Shawarma
food.desc: Damascene shawarma is thinly shaved beef or chicken with pickles, garlic toum and tahini, rolled in flatbread and pressed on the grill.

places.name: Station One
places.note: Well known modern shawarma counter in the embassy district, busy through the evening.

places.name: Al-Hamidiyah Souq stalls
places.note: Rows of shawarma spits along the covered souq, carved to order for a few coins.

places.name: Naranj
places.note: Sit-down version of the classics in one of the Old City's best known dining rooms.

food.name: Kibbeh
food.desc: Bulgur and minced meat shells stuffed with spiced lamb and pine nuts, fried, grilled or served raw as kibbeh nayyeh in Syrian mezze spreads.

places.name: Naranj
places.note: Polished Syrian kitchen on Straight Street with a wide kibbeh and mezze selection.

places.name: Al Khawali
places.note: Famous for both its food and its restored Damascene courtyard setting.

places.name: Beit Jabri
places.note: Traditional courtyard restaurant, a reliable place for grilled and fried kibbeh.

food.name: Booza (Damascene stretchy ice cream)
food.desc: Mastic and sahlab ice cream pounded with wooden mallets until elastic, rolled in crushed pistachios and eaten standing up.

places.name: Bakdash
places.note: Founded 1885 and still the icon; mallet-pounded booza served under a crowd of onlookers.

places.name: Bakdash Shaalan branch
places.note: Same booza away from the souq crush, handy if the main shop is jammed.

places.name: Souq booza counters near the Umayyad Mosque
places.note: Rival counters at the souq's end sell the same pistachio-rolled booza.

food.name: Damascene mezze
food.desc: A table of hummus, mutabbal, makdous stuffed aubergines, fattoush and warm bread; the standard opening act at any Old City restaurant.

places.name: Beit Jabri
places.note: Courtyard institution where the mezze spread is the reason to come.

places.name: Al Khawali
places.note: Generous traditional mezze in a grand restored merchant house.

places.name: Naranj
places.note: Upmarket Syrian cooking with a long and carefully made mezze list.

food.name: Barazek and Damascene sweets
food.desc: Sesame and pistachio barazek biscuits, halawet el-jibn cheese rolls and nut-stuffed maamoul, the city's centuries-old confectionery tradition.

places.name: Ghraoui
places.note: Historic Damascene confectioner, a name attached to the city's sweets for generations.

places.name: Semiramis Sweets
places.note: Well known sweet house for barazek, maamoul and syrup pastries by the kilo.

places.name: Al-Hamidiyah Souq sweet shops
places.note: Window after window of pistachio sweets sold by weight along the covered souq.

food.name: Tamarind sharab and jallab
food.desc: Chilled tamarind syrup poured by brass-tanked street vendors, and jallab of date molasses and rose water topped with pine nuts and raisins.

places.name: Al-Hamidiyah Souq drink vendors
places.note: Vendors in traditional dress pour tamarind from tanks strapped to their backs.

places.name: Umayyad Mosque gate vendors
places.note: Cold jallab and liquorice drinks sold to worshippers and visitors at the gates.

places.name: Bab Sharqi juice stands
places.note: Fresh juices plus tamarind and liquorice at the Old City's eastern gate.

food.name: Arabic coffee and mint tea
food.desc: Cardamom-scented qahwa in small cups, or sweet mint tea with a nargileh; the standard end to any Damascene meal.

places.name: Al-Nofara Cafe
places.note: Storyteller cafe behind the Umayyad Mosque, serving coffee and tea for over a century.

places.name: Beit Jabri
places.note: Courtyard coffee and nargileh, a favourite evening spot with Damascenes.

places.name: Naranj
places.note: Proper cardamom coffee to finish a meal on Straight Street.

landmarks: Umayyad Mosque
One of the world's oldest and largest mosques, its golden mosaics and vast marble courtyard make it Damascus's most revered and photographed monument.
Azm Palace
An 18th-century Ottoman-era palace with intricately carved wooden ceilings and tranquil courtyards, showcasing the opulence of Damascene aristocratic life.
Street Called Straight (Via Recta)
An ancient Roman colonnaded thoroughfare mentioned in the Bible, still lined with shops and historic buildings threading through the old city.
Citadel of Damascus
A massive medieval fortress guarding the edge of the old city, its imposing stone walls testify to centuries of Islamic and Ottoman military architecture.
Al-Hamidiyah Souq
A bustling, iron-roofed covered market stretching toward the Umayyad Mosque, alive with spice, textile, and sweet vendors beneath shafts of pierced light.
Chapel of Saint Paul (Bab Kisan)
A small, evocative chapel built into the ancient city walls marking where Saint Paul is said to have escaped Damascus in a basket.
National Museum of Damascus
Syria's premier museum, housing treasures spanning millennia from ancient Mesopotamia to Islamic art, behind a striking reconstructed desert-palace facade.
Mount Qasioun
A dramatic mountain overlooking the city, offering visitors panoramic views of Damascus's sprawling rooftops and minarets, especially stunning at dusk.
Mausoleum of Saladin
The final resting place of the legendary 12th-century sultan Saladin, a modest yet historically resonant tomb beside the Umayyad Mosque.
Bab Sharqi (Eastern Gate)
A Roman-era gate marking the eastern entrance to the old city, its weathered arch forming a gateway between antiquity and the bustling Christian quarter.

train.note: There is effectively no usable passenger rail. All long-distance and international trains remain suspended and the historic Hejaz station in the city centre is closed; the once-weekly sleepers from Istanbul and Tehran have not run for years. State operator CFS (Syrian Railways) runs only sporadic services. Travel in and out of Damascus is by road.

intl.to: Beirut (Lebanon) - 2-4 hr via the Masnaa border
intl.op: Kadmous / Al-Kamal — tickets at the Sumariyah international garage

intl.to: Amman (Jordan) - most of a day via the Nasib/Jaber border
intl.op: Kadmous / Al-Kamal — tickets at the Sumariyah international garage

bus.note: International coaches and shared taxis run mainly to Beirut (Lebanon, ~2-4h via the Masnaa border) and Amman (Jordan, most of a day via the Nasib/Jaber border), operated by Syrian carriers such as Kadmous and Al-Kamal; they leave from the Sumariyah (Somariyeh) international garage on the western edge of the city, and you buy tickets at the counters rather than online. The border with Turkey is generally closed to foreigners. Since the change of government in 2025, routes and schedules shift quickly - check locally before travelling.

ferry.note: Damascus is inland and has no ferries. Syria's Mediterranean ports are at Latakia and Tartus, but there is no regular scheduled international passenger ferry service from them.

half.name: Sidon
half.blurb: Ancient Phoenician port city on Lebanon's coast, rich in maritime history.

half.name: Tyre
half.blurb: Ancient Phoenician port city famed for its Roman ruins and long Mediterranean coastline.

full.blurb: Hilly capital city known for ancient ruins, bustling markets, and layered history.
